Engineering concept / design brief

100-Channel Battery Temperature Monitoring System

A consolidated design guide for monitoring the base temperature of approximately 100 × 14S battery packs while charging, including sensor selection, long-cable measurement, ADC/MCU options, isolation, modularization, circuit concepts, firmware, validation and buy-versus-build decisions.

100 temperature channels20–40 m per sensor cable (current assumption)NTC thermistorsCentral or distributed acquisitionPrototype before production
Engineering and safety status: This is a concept-level design guide, not a released schematic or certified battery-protection system. Component values are starting points. Validate against the exact battery, charger, grounding arrangement, cable, required accuracy and applicable safety/EMC requirements before operational use.

At a glance

Preferred sensor

10 kΩ NTC thermistor in an electrically insulated contact probe, with a documented resistance-temperature curve and specified tolerance.

Biggest architecture question

Does each NTC truly need 20–40 m of analog cable to the central cabinet, or can the measurement electronics be placed close to the batteries?

Centralized candidate

NTC divider + filtering/protection + multichannel ADCs + STM32-class MCU. Seven 16-channel ADCs provide 112 nominal channels for 100 sensors, if the selected ADC and bus topology fit.

More robust alternative

Short sensor leads into local acquisition modules, then isolated digital RS-485/CAN over the long distance.

2. Sensor technology and mounting

Why an NTC is the starting recommendation

An NTC thermistor's resistance decreases as its temperature rises. It is inexpensive, compact, sensitive over a limited range and can normally be read with a resistor divider and an ADC. A gain amplifier is usually unnecessary for this topology.

SensorBest fitTrade-offs for this project
10 kΩ NTCBattery/base temperature over a moderate rangeNonlinear curve; accuracy depends on sensor curve tolerance, mounting, cable leakage, divider design and calibration.
K-type thermocoupleHigh-temperature testing or very wide temperature rangeRequires thermocouple amplifier and cold-junction compensation; long low-level signal cable can be noise-sensitive.
J-type thermocoupleModerate high-temperature industrial applicationsNarrower useful range than K-type in many applications; iron leg can oxidize.
PTC thermistorThreshold protection or temperature-dependent switchingOften less suitable than NTC for precise continuous temperature measurement; behavior depends on exact PTC type.

Sensor purchase specification

  • Nominal resistance: 10 kΩ at 25°C.
  • Request the full resistance-temperature table or coefficients. “B3950” is only a candidate if the selected part's data sheet confirms it.
  • Check resistance tolerance and R–T curve tolerance separately; a 1% resistance tolerance alone does not guarantee 1% temperature accuracy.
  • Choose an insulated contact probe or flat sensor package with a suitable temperature range, response time, cable insulation and mechanical strain relief.
  • Use a mounting layer that provides repeatable thermal contact without damaging the battery or obstructing its cooling.
Mounting note: a metal base may spread heat and improve contact but can also couple heat between adjacent packs. An insulating base may slow response. Test both with a reference measurement before fixing the mechanical design.

3. Architecture choices

Option A — centralized analog acquisition

  • Advantages: one cabinet, centralized maintenance and one controller; no powered electronics beside batteries.
  • Disadvantages: 100 long analog cable pairs, many connectors, EMI susceptibility and more demanding input protection/fault diagnostics.
  • Use when: the full sensor cable run to the central cabinet is mandatory.

Option B — distributed measurement modules (preferred if cable constraint allows)

  • Use several identical modules, each reading 8–16 sensors; exact count depends on the selected channel count.
  • Keep NTC leads short and put ADC/MCU near the sensor groups.
  • Send digital measurements over an isolated multidrop bus where the grounding/safety assessment requires it.
  • This is usually the more robust architecture if “20–40 m” means the distance from the battery area to the controller rather than a mandatory analog cable per sensor.

Do you need an amplifier?

Usually not for a simple NTC divider. The ADC reads a voltage representing the thermistor resistance. A buffer or amplifier may be needed if source impedance, ADC sampling behavior, filter settling or accuracy requirements justify it. Amplifier offset, bias current, noise and common-mode range then enter the error budget.

5. Centralized NTC circuit concept

Important schematic note: This is a conceptual channel drawing, not a complete production schematic. Add connector-level protection, exact ADC reference wiring, decoupling, grounding and layout details from the chosen datasheets. Do not connect battery terminals to the analog ground. Use electrically insulated probes.

Measurement equation

For the divider shown, neglecting input loading and cable/series-resistor effects:

Vnode = VEXC × RNTC / (RFIXED + RNTC)

RNTC = RFIXED × Vnode / (VEXC − Vnode)

At 25°C, if both the NTC and fixed resistor are 10 kΩ and excitation is 2.5 V, the node is nominally 1.25 V. As an NTC warms, resistance usually falls, so this divider voltage falls. Use the selected sensor's R–T curve or validated Steinhart–Hart/B-parameter model to convert resistance to temperature.

For a ratiometric setup, measure the node relative to the same reference used for excitation. Confirm the selected ADC's allowed input range and reference requirements. A 12-bit ADC with a 2.5 V range has an ideal LSB of about 0.61 mV; actual temperature resolution depends on the divider slope, sensor curve, noise and calibration.

Filter and series-resistor selection

  • 1 kΩ series resistance and 10–100 nF are starting values for prototype experiments, not universal choices.
  • Compute the RC response using divider Thevenin resistance, cable capacitance, protection-device capacitance and ADC acquisition behavior.
  • Too much series resistance or capacitance can slow settling when a multiplexed ADC switches between channels.
  • Test the worst-case 40 m cable and charger-on noise. Do not assume filtering alone fixes conducted or common-mode interference.

6. Long-cable design: 20–40 m per sensor

Recommended wiring practice

  • Use a dedicated twisted pair per NTC; do not use the shield as the sensor return.
  • Keep sensor cables away from charger power cables, switching nodes, contactors and high-current conductors where practical.
  • Use keyed connectors, consistent pinout, channel labels and strain relief.
  • Shielding can help, but the shield termination must be chosen from the grounding topology and verified experimentally. A one-end shield bond is a test option, not a universal rule.
  • Check cable resistance, insulation leakage, cable capacitance, connector contamination and ESD/transient exposure.
  • Place low-leakage protection near the connector if needed. Check leakage current and capacitance because protection parts can bias high-impedance measurements.
Architecture trigger: if the 40 m analog cable causes unstable or inconsistent readings during charging, do not keep adding random capacitors. First evaluate routing and grounding, then consider a local measurement module with digital communication over the long cable.

7. ADC, MCU and digital interface

Centralized candidate: seven 16-channel ADCs

The TI ADS7953 is a 12-bit, 16-channel, multiplexed, single-ended SAR ADC with an SPI interface. Seven devices provide 112 nominal analog inputs, enough for 100 sensors with 12 spare channels. Verify the exact device revision, input range, reference wiring, SPI timing and output behavior in the current manufacturer datasheet.

SPI topology caution: use a shared clock/data arrangement only if the ADC's output-enable/tri-state behavior permits it. Otherwise use separate data-return lines or a suitable buffer/multiplexer. Verify this against the datasheet rather than assuming all ADC MISO pins can be tied together.

MCU firmware responsibilities

  • Scan each channel on a documented schedule and allow ADC settling after channel changes as required.
  • Convert ADC codes to resistance, then temperature using the sensor-specific curve.
  • Store raw and filtered readings; do not filter so heavily that rapid temperature rises are hidden.
  • Maintain channel identity, timestamp, sensor status, last-good value and alarm state.
  • Detect open/short circuits, out-of-range readings, stale data, ADC communication faults and MCU resets.
  • Use a watchdog and define the charging interlock's state on reset, loss of communications or loss of system power.

8. Isolation and grounding

Isolation is not one generic component. Define the required isolation boundary from the battery/charger electrical arrangement, potential differences, grounding, transients and safety requirements.

BoundaryGuidance
Sensor to analog circuitA passive NTC can share a measurement domain if the probe is appropriately insulated and the safety analysis permits it. Confirm the probe's insulation rating and mounting.
Between battery channelsIf packs have different ground potentials or conductive mounting can create paths, a shared-ground central design may be unsuitable. Consider isolated local modules or isolated channel/group front ends.
MCU to host / long digital busAn isolated RS-485 transceiver is a candidate if the host link needs isolation. This does not isolate the analog inputs from each other.
Power across isolation barrierSignal isolation alone may not be enough; use appropriately rated isolated power when the isolated domain requires it.
Charging stopDo not rely only on a software dashboard. The fault-safe charging-stop path needs an independent design and validation appropriate to the system.
Do not finalize the shared-ground schematic yet if the relationship between chargers, battery packs, metal bases and protective earth is unknown. Establish the grounding and common-mode conditions first. Isolation voltage, creepage/clearance and transient ratings must be selected from the actual installation requirements.

9. Firmware, alarms and fault behavior

Minimum channel states

StatusExample detectionExpected system response
ValidReading inside plausible operating range and stable communicationLog and display temperature and trend.
Open sensor / cableADC near expected open-circuit rail or resistance beyond valid rangeMark sensor fault; do not treat as safe temperature.
Shorted sensor / cableADC near zero or resistance below valid rangeMark sensor fault; trigger configured protective response.
OvertemperatureTemperature exceeds manufacturer-based warning/trip thresholdAlarm and command the validated safe charging stop.
Stale reading / bus failureNo valid update within defined timeoutMark data invalid; notify operator and invoke fault policy.
Controller reset / watchdogStartup/reset cause or heartbeat missingInterlock should move to the predefined safe state where required.

Alarm thresholds cannot be safely chosen from a generic example. Use the battery manufacturer's permitted charging temperature range for the exact chemistry, pack design and charging profile. Include sensor placement lag and measurement uncertainty in the threshold margin.

10. Battery safety and thermal validation

  • A base sensor is not equivalent to an internal cell sensor. A cell can heat internally before the base temperature changes substantially.
  • Validate sensor lag under worst-case charging conditions and compare readings against a trusted reference measurement at relevant pack locations.
  • Do not puncture, compress, abrade or obstruct cooling of the battery pack during sensor mounting.
  • Keep sensor wiring mechanically secure and electrically insulated from battery terminals and conductive bases.
  • Determine how the system stops charging safely on overtemperature, sensor failure, controller failure and communications loss.
  • Perform an electrical safety and EMC review before operational deployment. The appropriate standards depend on the equipment, battery, charger and installation.

Recommended buy/build split

Buy

  • NTC probes
  • Industrial cable and connectors
  • ADC evaluation board
  • MCU development board
  • Isolated transceiver module for prototype
  • Reference thermometer / calibration equipment

Design in-house later

  • Channel front-end PCB
  • Channel identification and diagnostics
  • Firmware and logging
  • Host software / dashboard
  • Production test fixtures

Practical recommendation: buy the sensor probes and evaluation hardware first. Build a 4-channel proof-of-concept with the actual 40 m cable. Compare it with a commercial multichannel module that explicitly supports your selected NTC. Then choose custom PCB versus complete modules based on measured accuracy, fault behavior, integration effort and total cost—not the purchase price alone.

12. Prototype and verification plan

1
Define the real requirements.
Confirm chemistry, manufacturer charging limits, required accuracy, sampling rate, cable length, grounding and isolation boundary.
2
Buy a small set of parts.
Order 6–10 candidate NTC probes, representative 40 m cables/connectors, a suitable ADC evaluation board and an STM32 development board.
3
Build 4 channels.
Use footprints/options for resistor and capacitor changes. Include input protection footprints and test points.
4
Calibrate and test the cable.
Compare against a reference thermometer at multiple temperatures; test cable routing, charger on/off noise, contact repeatability and response lag.
5
Inject faults.
Disconnect and short each sensor; test intermittent wiring, ADC faults, communication loss, MCU reset and power failure.
6
Choose the architecture.
Use centralized analog only if long sensor runs are mandatory and tests show adequate robustness. Otherwise prefer local measurement plus isolated digital bus.
7
Scale gradually.
Move from 4 channels to an 8–16-channel module, then to 100 channels after validation and safety review.

100-Channel Battery
Temperature Monitoring System

Concept architecture, hardware selection, circuit design, firmware, isolation and validation

Project parameterCurrent assumption
Battery populationApproximately 100 battery packs
Pack configuration14S; chemistry and exact pack voltage not yet confirmed
Sensor placementOne temperature sensor beneath each battery, at its base/contact surface
Wiring20–40 m per sensor to central electronics, for the centralized design

Purpose: consolidate the discussed design into a working engineering brief. The circuit and BOM are starting points; they are not a validated production design.

1. Executive summary

The system monitors one temperature point beneath each of approximately 100 14S battery packs during charging. The present constraint is a 20–40 m cable from each sensor to the central electronics. A 10 kΩ NTC thermistor is the recommended starting sensor because it is inexpensive, sensitive around normal battery temperatures, and easy to measure using a resistor divider and ADC. An amplifier is usually unnecessary for an NTC divider.

Two architectures were discussed. The centralized analog architecture keeps all 100 sensor inputs, filters and ADCs at one cabinet, but long analog cables make noise, leakage, ground-reference and protection design important. The preferred architecture from a robustness standpoint is distributed measurement near the batteries, with short NTC leads and a long isolated digital RS-485/CAN bus. That alternative only works if the 20–40 m requirement can apply to the digital link rather than every sensor's analog cable.

• Initial sensor: insulated 10 kΩ NTC probe with a documented R–T curve; B value such as B3950 only if the selected part's datasheet confirms it.
• Central ADC example: seven 16-channel ADS7953 ADCs give 112 inputs, of which 100 can be used.
• Controller example: STM32G474 or another suitable STM32; a Nucleo development board is useful during prototyping.
• Communications example: isolated RS-485 transceiver such as ADM2587E for a host/digital link; this does not isolate the analog sensor channels.
• Safety: a base-temperature sensor can lag the hottest cell. Use manufacturer-defined temperature limits and an independent, fault-safe charging-stop mechanism.

3. Sensor technology decision

Sensor typeStrengthsLimitationsAssessment for this project
10 kΩ NTC thermistorLow cost, high sensitivity over a limited range, simple ADC interfaceNonlinear R–T curve; resistance and cable leakage affect reading; temperature range limited by partRecommended starting point

Sensor specification to request from suppliers:

• Nominal resistance: 10 kΩ at 25°C.
• Documented resistance-temperature table or coefficients; confirm B value instead of assuming B3950.
• Resistance tolerance and curve tolerance stated separately; 1% nominal resistance tolerance is a reasonable target, but curve tolerance also matters.
• Insulated probe/contact surface suitable for placement under the battery; cable insulation and strain relief suitable for the charging environment.
• Response time, temperature range, long-term stability, and insulation rating documented.
• Select a mounting method that gives repeatable contact pressure without damaging the pack or obstructing its cooling.

4. System architecture options

4.1 Option A — centralized analog acquisition

Each sensor has a dedicated two-conductor cable up to 20–40 m long, terminating at a central PCB. The PCB contains connector protection, a divider and filter per channel, ADCs, an STM32, and a host interface. This meets the current interpretation that every sensor cable must run the full distance, but it is the more demanding design for analog noise.

• Advantages: all electronics in one cabinet; one controller; easier central servicing; no powered remote modules.
• Disadvantages: 100 long analog cable pairs; connector count; cable pickup and ground-return concerns; more input protection and diagnostics; potentially difficult calibration and fault localization.

4.2 Option B — distributed measurement modules (preferred if allowed)

Place local measurement modules close to groups of batteries. Each module reads a group of NTCs using local dividers, filters and an ADC, then sends digital readings to the central controller over isolated RS-485 or CAN. This changes the long cable from a sensitive analog measurement cable into a differential digital communications cable.

• Possible scale: 7–13 modules for groups of 8–16 sensors, depending on channel count and layout.
• Advantages: shorter analog wiring, better noise immunity, easier fault isolation, modular maintenance.
• Disadvantages: remote power, enclosures, firmware and environmental protection are required; the long cable is no longer each sensor’s analog cable.

4.3 Architecture decision

If the requirement truly mandates 20–40 m from every NTC to the central PCB, proceed with Option A and validate it under real charging conditions. If the requirement instead describes the distance from each battery area to the controller, Option B is recommended.

6. Single-channel circuit concept

The circuit shown is conceptual. A production schematic must add the actual connector pinout, input protection, proper ADC reference connections, decoupling, grounding and PCB layout. The simplified divider uses a 2.5 V excitation and a 10 kΩ fixed resistor above the sense node, with the NTC connected from the sense node to the analog return. If the ADC reference is the same 2.5 V source, the measurement is ratiometric.

6.1 Nominal behavior

• At 25°C, a 10 kΩ NTC and 10 kΩ fixed resistor produce approximately half the excitation voltage: 1.25 V with 2.5 V excitation.
• As temperature increases, NTC resistance usually decreases, so this divider’s sense voltage decreases.
• With the same excitation and ADC reference, the ratio is approximately VADC/VREF = RNTC/(Rfixed + RNTC), subject to input loading and series components.
• Convert the measured ratio to resistance, then temperature using the actual sensor’s R–T table or validated Steinhart–Hart/B-parameter model.
• An open sensor tends toward the upper measurement limit; a shorted sensor tends toward zero. These must be flagged as faults.

6.2 Series resistor and capacitor

A 1 kΩ series resistor and 10–100 nF capacitor were discussed as initial filter/protection candidates. They are not universal values. The filter must be analyzed with the divider’s source impedance, cable capacitance, ADC input sampling behavior and channel scan rate. Too much series resistance or capacitance can slow settling and bias multiplexed ADC readings if acquisition time is insufficient.

6.3 Cable and grounding

• Use one twisted pair per sensor; route it away from charger input/output cables and switching nodes.
• Shielding may help, but the shield termination strategy must be decided from the grounding topology. Avoid accidentally creating ground loops.
• Do not connect battery terminals to measurement ground. Use electrically insulated probes and verify the probe’s insulation rating.
• Long cable leakage, connector contamination, induced transients and common-mode voltages can create measurement error or damage.
• Consider fault-detection bias paths or diagnostics that can distinguish a plausible temperature from open/short wiring faults.

6.4 ADC bank and SPI

• Seven ADS7953 devices offer 112 single-ended inputs; use 100 and reserve 12 channels.
• A shared SPI clock/data bus with one chip-select per ADC is a possible arrangement; check the exact timing and interface requirements in the current datasheet.
• Provide local decoupling and a clean analog layout around each ADC. Separate noisy digital return currents from sensitive analog input paths, then join grounds according to the IC layout guidance.
• Confirm ADC input range, reference pin requirements, input settling and SPI timing before freezing the schematic.

7. Amplifier decision

An NTC thermistor is a resistive sensor, so a divider plus ADC is normally sufficient. A gain amplifier is not inherently required. An op-amp buffer can be useful if the source impedance, ADC acquisition behavior, or filtering calls for it, but its offset, bias current, input common-mode range, noise and stability must be included in the error budget.

If a higher-precision ADC with a programmable-gain amplifier is desired, the Analog Devices AD7124-8 is an alternative candidate for smaller channel groups. It is a 24-bit sigma-delta ADC with PGA features, but it is not automatically more accurate at the system level, and 100 channels would require many devices or a distributed architecture.

8. Isolation strategy

Isolation boundaryGuidance
Sensor to central analog circuitA passive NTC does not itself require an isolation amplifier if the probe is insulated, all channels may share the same safe analog domain, and the safety analysis permits it.
Between battery sensor circuitsIf battery packs can have different potentials, exposed conductive bases, or different charger-ground references, a shared-ground centralized design may be unsuitable. Consider isolated local modules or isolated channel/group front ends.
MCU to host / long digital busAn isolated RS-485 interface such as ADM2587E is a candidate. Integrated signal/power isolation simplifies the interface, but confirm isolation rating and layout rules.
Power crossing an isolation barrierDigital isolation alone is insufficient. Any required isolated domain also needs appropriately rated isolated power.
Protective charging stopDo not depend solely on the main MCU/dashboard. The stop path and fault response need a separate safety review and appropriate hardware.

The correct isolation voltage, creepage/clearance, transient rating and number of isolated domains cannot be determined until the charger grounding, battery electrical arrangement, maximum common-mode voltage and applicable safety requirements are known.

9. Firmware and data processing

• Acquire each ADC channel with a known scan schedule; discard or delay readings as needed after multiplexed-channel switching to allow settling.
• Apply a documented conversion method using the sensor-specific R–T curve. Avoid assuming every NTC has the same B value.
• Filter noise without hiding rapid temperature increases; keep both raw and filtered readings for diagnostics.
• Track per-channel status: valid, open circuit, short circuit, out of range, stale reading, ADC/communication fault.
• Record channel identity, timestamp, temperature, fault state and alarm state.
• Use manufacturer-specified charge-temperature limits to configure warnings and trips; thresholds are not specified in this document.
• On sensor fault or overtemperature, raise a clear alarm and command a safe charging stop through the defined interlock.
• On MCU reset, watchdog timeout, communications loss or power failure, the charging interlock should fail to a defined safe state where the system requirements demand it.

10. Base mounting and thermal validation

The sensor is under the battery, so it measures the base/contact area rather than the internal cell temperature. Metal can spread heat and improve contact but can also couple heat between batteries; an insulating base may slow response or create a different temperature gradient. The mounting choice must be tested with the final battery, base, clamping pressure, pad/adhesive, airflow and charging current.

• Use an electrically insulating sensor package or mounting layer appropriate to the battery’s electrical environment.
• Avoid compressing, puncturing or mechanically stressing the battery pack.
• Test worst-case charging conditions and compare base-sensor readings with a trusted reference measurement at relevant pack locations.
• Determine the lag between cell heating and base sensor detection. Set alarm/trip thresholds only after this lag is understood.
• Ensure a sensor cannot be dislodged without being detected or producing a clear maintenance fault.

11. Prototype and verification plan

Build a 4-channel prototype with the intended NTC probe, divider, protection, ADC and MCU.
Test at least one 40 m cable with the actual connector and shield arrangement.
Calibrate against a reference thermometer at several points across the intended charging temperature range.
Measure repeatability, offset, drift, response time and error after cable installation.
Operate the intended chargers and nearby equipment during testing; record noise and transient behavior.
Inject open circuit, short circuit, intermittent contact, disconnected ADC, SPI fault and MCU reset conditions.
Test the charging-stop/interlock path independently of the software dashboard.
Validate the final mounting on both candidate base materials, then select the base based on thermal response and safety.
Scale from 4 channels to a small multi-ADC board, then to 100 channels after the test results are acceptable.
Perform an electrical safety and EMC review before operational deployment.

12. Risks and unresolved decisions

Open decisionWhy it matters / next action
Battery chemistry and manufacturer temperature limitsRequired to set operating range, alarm/trip thresholds and sensor qualification.
Meaning of 20–40 m cableIf each NTC must run that full length to the central PCB, use centralized analog design; if distance is only to the battery area, distributed digital acquisition is preferred.
Electrical relation between packs and chargersDetermines whether sensor circuits can share a ground or need channel/group isolation.
Base material and sensor mountingChanges thermal lag, heat spreading, contact repeatability and alarm behavior.
Required temperature accuracy and sampling rateDetermines sensor tolerance, ADC resolution, calibration, filtering and scan schedule.
Host interface and loggingChoose USB, Ethernet, isolated RS-485, CAN, PLC or PC integration after system requirements are clear.
Applicable safety and EMC standardsMust be identified before production design, especially for charging interlock and isolation.

13. Preliminary engineering recommendation

Proceed with a 4-channel prototype using insulated 10 kΩ NTC probes and a ratiometric divider. Use the actual 40 m cable and the intended charger environment. For a centralized design, evaluate ADS7953-based acquisition and an STM32 controller; seven 16-channel ADCs cover 100 inputs. Add input protection and fault diagnostics after the cable/grounding assessment. Use isolated RS-485 for a digital host link if appropriate, while recognizing that this does not isolate the analog sensor channels.

Before committing to the 100-channel PCB, decide whether the system needs isolation per sensor, per group, or only at the host interface. If each sensor’s analog cable can be shortened, reconsider distributed acquisition because it is generally the more robust arrangement for long distances.

14. Expanded component recommendations and detailed circuit implementation

This section adds practical component-level suggestions and implementation notes to the earlier concept document. Part numbers and values are candidates for engineering evaluation, not a released BOM. Verify current datasheets, availability, electrical limits and layout requirements before schematic capture or ordering.

14.1 Recommended centralized channel circuit

Recommended starting topology: a fixed resistor from a stable excitation rail to the sense node; the NTC from that node to the sensor return; a series resistor between the sense node and ADC input; and a capacitor at the ADC input to analog ground. Use the same excitation/reference for a ratiometric arrangement where supported by the selected ADC. The diagram is simplified and omits connector-level ESD protection and all layout-specific details.

ReferenceStarting componentPurpose / design notes
NTC110 kΩ NTC at 25°C; documented curve; insulated probeSelect tolerance, B/curve tolerance, thermal time constant, insulation rating and cable construction.
R110.0 kΩ, 0.1%, low tempcoForms divider. A precision resistor helps but does not remove NTC curve tolerance or mounting error.
R21 kΩ initial evaluation valueSeries impedance for input protection/filtering. Verify interaction with ADC input sampling and channel settling.
C110–100 nF initial evaluation rangeLow-pass filter at ADC input. Determine final value from noise, source impedance, cable capacitance and scan rate.
D1/D2Low-leakage ESD/TVS protection appropriate to the input rangePlace near connector if cable exposure warrants it. Leakage must be small relative to divider currents; select clamping voltage and capacitance carefully.
J1Keyed 2-pin connector or terminal blockLabel sensor + and return consistently; provide strain relief and prevent miswiring.
VEXC/VREF2.5 V precision reference or validated ratiometric excitationUse only after verifying selected ADC reference and input ranges. Add recommended bypass capacitor(s) from the reference datasheet.
AGNDAnalog return plane/domainKeep the sensor circuit in a defined domain. Do not connect battery terminals to AGND.

14.2 Calculation example

For Rfixed = 10 kΩ and RNTC = 10 kΩ at 25°C, Vnode = VEXC × RNTC / (Rfixed + RNTC). With VEXC = 2.5 V, Vnode = 1.25 V. As an NTC warms, its resistance normally falls and this divider voltage falls. For a ratiometric measurement, RNTC can be estimated as Rfixed × Vnode / (VEXC − Vnode), subject to the actual topology, loading and series-resistor location. Convert resistance using the specific sensor curve.

The fixed-resistor value should be checked against the sensor's expected resistance range and target temperature range. The divider must keep the ADC input within its permitted range at all temperatures and during open/short faults. Calculate resistor dissipation and NTC self-heating, and avoid excessive sensor current.

14.3 Cable-entry protection and long-cable notes

• At each connector, consider low-leakage ESD protection and series impedance suitable for the expected ESD/transient environment. Do not select a generic TVS without checking leakage, capacitance, working voltage and clamping voltage.
• Use twisted pair. If shielded cable is selected, define shield bonding deliberately; one-end bonding is a common starting test, not a universal rule. Validate the grounding strategy on the actual charger installation.
• Cable copper resistance is usually less problematic than leakage, induced interference, connector contamination and ground offsets for a high-impedance NTC divider, but it must still be included in the error budget.
• Long cable capacitance combined with divider/source impedance can slow response and ADC settling. Test worst-case cable type and length, especially at 40 m.
• If measurements shift when chargers switch, compare shielded/unshielded tests, improve routing and filtering, and consider moving the analog front end close to the sensors.
• Do not use the shield as the NTC return conductor. Keep signal return and shield functions distinct unless the validated system design explicitly specifies otherwise.

14.4 ADC and MCU interconnection

Signal / blockImplementation guidance
SPI SCLKRoute to all ADS7953 devices; check total bus capacitance and timing.
SPI MOSIShared command/configuration path from MCU to ADCs.
SPI MISOShared return only if device tri-state behavior and datasheet requirements permit; otherwise use separate MISO lines or a suitable mux/buffer.
CS per ADCSeven separate chip-select signals for seven ADCs; GPIO expanders are possible but add timing/complexity.
ADC supply and decouplingUse local bypass capacitors as specified by the datasheet, placed close to supply pins.
Reference/excitationDecouple per reference datasheet; route carefully and verify load-drive capability for all divider channels.
Grounding/layoutKeep analog inputs and reference away from fast digital traces; follow ADC evaluation-board layout guidance where available.
Host linkUART/USB/Ethernet or isolated RS-485 as system integration requires; host isolation does not isolate sensor inputs.

Before finalizing a shared MISO bus, verify ADS7953 output-state behavior during deselection in the current datasheet. If multiple ADC outputs can drive MISO simultaneously, use separate MISO lines or a bus-switch/multiplexer architecture rather than connecting outputs together.

14.5 Power and reference design

• Choose the 3.3 V regulator based on total MCU, ADC, interface and status-indicator current, thermal dissipation, transient response and input supply range.
• A low-noise LDO such as the TPS7A20 family is a candidate for a low-current 3.3 V rail, but calculate its dropout, dissipation and current headroom from the actual BOM.
• A precision reference should be selected for initial accuracy, drift, output drive, noise and stability with its capacitive load. Do not assume a reference can drive 100 divider branches without checking the datasheet.
• If excitation current is too large for a reference, use a suitable buffer or separate excitation supply and measure that excitation ratiometrically. Validate reference loading and ADC reference requirements.
• Separate analog and digital supply filtering as recommended by the ADC/MCU manufacturers. Avoid improvised ground splits; use a deliberate return-current layout.

14.6 Isolation circuit options

RequirementCandidate approachNotes
Only PC/host bus needs isolationADM2587E isolated RS-485, or a digital isolator plus isolated DC/DCAppropriate if all analog sensor channels may safely share one measurement domain.
Groups of sensors need isolation from hostLocal ADC/MCU module per group + isolated RS-485/CANKeep NTC leads short; long run becomes digital. Isolated power may be required.
Each sensor circuit needs isolationIsolated analog measurement per channel or isolated local modules grouped according to the safety analysis100 independent isolation barriers can add substantial cost/area; do not decide without common-mode and fault analysis.
Battery/charger ground relationship unknownDo not release the shared-ground schematic yetMeasure/establish electrical relationships and consult relevant safety requirements before choosing the isolation boundary.

The ADM2587E is an example isolated RS-485 transceiver, not an isolated 100-channel analog front end. Isolation ratings, creepage/clearance, surge performance and isolated power must be checked against the final installation requirements.

14.7 Distributed measurement module circuit (alternative)

If the long-distance requirement can be met by a digital bus, build a local module for each group of 8–16 sensors. Each module can use the same NTC divider principle, a suitable multichannel ADC or MCU ADC, a local controller, and an isolated RS-485/CAN interface. The long cable then carries differential digital data and power only if the power design allows it. This usually improves immunity compared with 100 long analog runs.

Module blockCandidate direction
Analog channels8–16 NTC divider channels, local RC filtering and connector protection.
ADCA multichannel ADC selected for required accuracy, or an MCU with sufficient ADC inputs and validated performance.
Local MCUSTM32 or another supported MCU with watchdog, diagnostics and bus protocol.
Digital busRS-485 for simple multidrop topology; CAN where its protocol/diagnostics and system requirements justify it.
IsolationIsolated transceiver and isolated supply where required by grounding and safety assessment.
PowerProtected low-voltage supply sized for module and sensors; assess whether power can share the cable or needs local supply.

14.8 Suggested purchasing and prototype sequence

Order 6–10 NTC probes from one candidate supplier, plus the exact intended 40 m cable and connectors.
Build 4 analog channels with 10 kΩ 0.1% resistors, selectable R2 values, selectable filter capacitors and connector protection footprints.
Prototype one ADS7953 channel group or evaluation board and an STM32 Nucleo controller before designing a 100-channel PCB.
Use a calibrated reference thermometer and a controlled temperature source to build a calibration/error budget.
Test charger-on/charger-off noise, cable routing, sensor open/short, transient immunity and startup behavior.
Choose central analog or distributed digital architecture based on test data and the final isolation requirement.
Only then release the 100-channel BOM, schematic, PCB and production test procedure.

14.9 Design-release checklist

• Battery chemistry, charging profile and manufacturer temperature limits documented.
• Exact NTC part number and R–T curve approved.
• Maximum 40 m cable and connector details frozen.
• Base material, sensor placement and thermal lag measured.
• Isolation boundary and grounding strategy approved.
• ADC reference/input range, settling time and SPI topology verified against datasheets.
• Input protection leakage and transient rating verified.
• Open/short and communications fault behavior tested.
• Independent safe charging stop tested.
• EMC, electrical safety, enclosure, creepage/clearance and serviceability reviewed.
